This Is the Ford That Inspired Jason's First Car in GTA 6: Meet the Vapid Ganado
14 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
The Vapid Ganado is the car on everybody’s lips these days, and it’s not even a real model. The GTA 6 craze has reached the level where people are searching the web for ways to buy a Ganado, and to everyone’s surprise, this is a car that you can actually buy and drive.
Well, sort of, as nobody has ever created a Vapid Ganado as you know it from the new Grand Theft Auto . But the Ganado is based on a vehicle that actually existed, and if money isn’t an issue, you should be able to find out in good shape online.
The Ganado is the first car you get in GTA 6. It’s not the most eye-candy truck, but on the other hand, it serves its purpose quite right. Considering it’s a pickup, you use it to carry stuff around, such as Lucia’s clothes when she gets out of prison, groceries, your loadout, and so on.
This is precisely how the model that the Ganado is based on was born.
Photo: Ford Enter the Ford Ranchero.
The Ranchero came to be in 1957 when Ford was still the number one carmaker in the United States. Things were about to change in 1958, when Chevrolet secured the leading spot, but the introduction of the Ranchero made perfect sense for people who wanted a good-looking car with a utilitarian upgrade.
Based on Ford’s full-size platform, the Ranchero sported the front of full-size cars mixed with a pickup-like bed in the back. It was powered by the same engines as its full-size siblings, beginning with a 223 six and ending with the 292 and the 352 V8s.
The Ranchero was so popular that Chevrolet had no other option but to come up with a model of its own specifically to compete with it. The El Camino was based on the same approach, with the full-size platform spearheaded by the Impala serving as the development platform.
However, the El Camino wasn’t as popular as the Ranchero, and it was pulled after only two years. It was reintroduced in 1964 as part of Chevrolet’s existing lineups.
The Ranchero survived and continued to command a significant customer share.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The Ranchero lineup was expanded in 1970, when Ford added the Squire - a more luxurious version of the pickup truck - and the GT - whose main focus was the performance under the hood. Each model came with unique features and more or less powerful engines, depending on the audience they were going after.
For example, the GT could be ordered with a 429 Cobra Jet with a shaker hood air scoop, Ram Air induction, and the performance handling package. The top configuration produced no more, no less than 370 horsepower.
Ford did not want the Ranchero to lose its utilitarian purpose despite going for more powerful and more luxurious options.
The base version was still fitted with a 200 ci six-cylinder engine that developed only 155 horsepower. This engine made sense for people who wanted the Ranchero for actual work.
The V8 offering started with a 302 rated at 220 horsepower and continued with a 351 that could be had with a two-barrel or a four-barrel carburetor. These engines produced 250 and 300 horsepower, respectively.
The 429 was available in two configurations: the Thunder Jet with 360 horsepower and the Cobra with 370 horsepower.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Theoretically, the Ganado is offered with a 434 engine, as indicated by the tags on the side of the truck. You can see these tags in the photos I took with the Ganado in its standard configuration. The yellow paint is the one I applied for free, though Ultimate buyers can also customize the vehicle with the Retro Build for free.
Obviously, you can customize the Ganado even further as you play the game, as there are lots of options, beginning with the engine under the hood and ending with the wheels and other cosmetic improvements. They all cost serious dollars, so you’ll have to work quite a lot for Brian to be able to afford all of these.
However, the Ganado is proving to be quite an efficient ride for Jason, especially in the first chapters in the game. It’ll end up coming in handy after Lucia is released from prison, too, but I’m with most players here - the more you play, the more tempted you are to purchase another car.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution So there you go, if you’re such a big fan of the Ganado, you can actually build one yourself if you get a 1970 Ranchero project car. These cars shouldn’t cost more than a couple of thousand dollars, considering they aren’t necessarily the most sought-after.
Of course, you won’t get a tip-top shape at this price, but a running engine and a bed that can still hold your stuff without falling through the rust holes should be doable at $2,000.
